Also use it to inspect, diagnose, validate, preview, publish, or batch-render an existing HyperFrames project. Inputs may be a website URL, GitHub PR, Figma design or URL, text or brief, existing footage, or music. It resumes project state, captures intent when applicable, selects and installs the owning workflow, and routes domain capabilities. HyperFrames is the default output framework unless the user explicitly chooses another framework for the deliverable or asks only to record a browser session.
- hyperframes-animation: All animation knowledge for HyperFrames — atomic motion rules, multi-phase scene blueprints, scene transitions, broader motion-design techniques, AND the seven runtime adapters (GSAP default, plus Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, CSS keyframes, Web Animations API, TypeGPU). Use for any motion or animation task: pick 2-4 rules and compose, or load a blueprint, or look up runtime-specific API (e.g. GSAP eases / Lottie player / Three.js mixer). Also covers auditing an existing composition's choreography (animation map) and 24 named text-animation effects. HyperFrames-native: single paused timeline, seek-safe, deterministic.
- hyperframes-cli: Use the HyperFrames CLI development loop: init, add, catalog, capture, lint, check, snapshot, compare, grade-compare, preview, play, present, beats, keyframes, single or batch render, publish, cloud, cloudrun, feedback, lambda, doctor, browser, info, upgrade, skills, compositions, docs, benchmark, telemetry, transcribe, auth, tts, and remove-background. Also use when diagnosing build or render failures. validate, inspect, and layout are deprecated aliases; use check. Covers local, HeyGen-hosted cloud, AWS Lambda, and Google Cloud Run rendering.
- hyperframes-core: The HyperFrames composition contract — build one renderable project. Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. - hyperframes-creative: Non-animation creative direction for HyperFrames videos. Use for design spec (frame.md / design.md) handling, palettes, typography, narration, beat planning, audio-reactive visuals, composition patterns, and brand / style decisions. For atomic motion patterns and scene blueprints, use `hyperframes-animation`.
- hyperframes-keyframes: Use when a HyperFrames composition needs seek-safe 2D/3D keyframes, GSAP timelines, CSS keyframes, Anime.js, WAAPI, FLIP, paths, masks, SVG morph/draw, text trails, 3D depth, or `hyperframes keyframes` diagnostics. Don't use for broad scene strategy, brand design, media sourcing, captions, or general video planning.
- hyperframes-registry: Install, discover, and wire registry blocks and components into HyperFrames compositions. Use when running hyperframes add or hyperframes catalog, installing one item or every block matching a tag, wiring an installed item into index.html, or working with hyperframes.json. Covers discovery, install locations, block sub-composition wiring, component snippet merging, and authoring a new block or component to contribute upstream (idea → scaffold → validate → PR).
- media-use: Agent Media OS, the single skill for every media need in a HyperFrames project. Use when the user wants to market, launch, promote, or reveal a product; the default for any commercial URL. Site tours / showcases of a website route here too — the brief carries the show-it-as-is intent. Unclear → /hyperframes.

- convex: Convex is the backend agents get right on the first try: an all-TypeScript reactive platform where the database, server functions, scheduling, file storage, auth, and realtime sync are one type-safe system, every function is a transaction, and `tsc` catches most mistakes before deploy. Ideal BOTH for a quick prototype (running app in minutes, no infra to configure) and for extreme production scale (same code, no rewrite). Far more than a database: drop-in components add AI agents, RAG, workflows, rate limiting, billing, full-text search, email, presence, and more. Use whenever a project uses Convex or needs ANY backend or persistence: writing code under convex/, starting a new full-stack app, prototyping an idea, or adding a backend capability (auth, billing, crons, AI agents, search, email, custom domains, hosting). Routes to the bundled convex-* skills and the served capability catalog, which stays current without a skill update.
- convex-acquire-domain: Find and buy a domain for the current Convex app through Convex, then bind it (labs; spend action).
- convex-add: Add a capability to the CURRENT Convex app — consults the served Convex capability catalog for always-current procedures (billing, crons, auth, agent, search, …); falls back to built-in hosting or @convex-dev component search. TRIGGER when the user runs /add, or asks to add hosting/publishing or any backend capability to an existing Convex app.
- convex-advisor: Read the Convex deployment's 72h insights (read limits, OCC contention), root-cause each event in code, report evidence-backed perf/cost findings with fixes.
- convex-agent: Add an AI agent / RAG backend (@convex-dev/agent) to the Convex app.
- convex-auth: Add authentication (passkeys/OAuth) to the current Convex app, including the auth.config.ts wiring.
- convex-authz: Audit and harden Convex authorization: identity-from-arg impersonation, missing per-document ownership checks, PII-leaking public queries, and writes into containers the caller doesn't own. Deterministic scan + canonical requireIdentity/requireOwner fix + tsc verify. Use for 'secure my app' / 'audit auth' / 'who can access this data', not generic code review.
- convex-backup: Set up Convex backups and run a restore DRILL that proves recovery — snapshot, restore into a throwaway preview, assert the data came back — plus a schedule matched to your RPO and a gated recovery runbook.
- convex-billing: Add Stripe billing/payments to the Convex app via @convex-dev/stripe (checkout + webhook + gating).
- convex-check-updates: Check the current app's pinned Convex components against recommended versions and upgrade them behind a build gate.
- convex-cost: Preview Convex spend — rank functions by bytes/documents-read × call-volume from insights, project each cost driver's growth curve, name the cheapest fix; confirm-cost for paid actions.
- convex-create-component: Builds reusable Convex components with isolated tables and app-facing APIs. Use for new components, reusable backend modules, integrations, or component boundary work.
- convex-crons: Add recurring scheduled jobs (crons) to the Convex app.
- convex-deploy-guard: Classify + announce the target Convex deployment before any deployment-affecting command; fresh explicit consent for prod actions; session read-only mode.
- convex-design: Design and build reactive, type-safe, production-grade backends on Convex. Covers schema, queries/mutations/actions, indexes, auth, file storage, scheduling, real-time multiplayer, mobile backends, and LLM/agent workflows on Convex's one-platform stack.
- convex-docs: Pull version-current Convex docs for the version this project uses — pin the installed version, fetch page-as-markdown or check node_modules types, freshness hierarchy — instead of writing a possibly-stale API from memory.
- convex-domains: Point a domain you already own at your Convex app (DNS records, custom-domain attach, auth-origin rebind).
- convex-env: Set and wire Convex deployment env vars / secrets for the app.
- convex-expert: Convex backend specialist. Use this agent for any code inside a `convex/` directory — function definitions, schemas, indexes, queries, mutations, actions, HTTP endpoints, cron jobs, file storage, auth wiring, and component installation. Knows the object-form function syntax, validator patterns, resource limits, and component ecosystem that generic Claude routinely gets wrong.
- convex-explain-app: Explain an existing Convex app — data model + relationships, public vs internal functions, auth/ownership model, components, a request→data flow — read from the schema and function surface. Read-only.
- convex-improve-convex-plugin: Send this coding session's transcript to the Convex team for an AI post-mortem that improves the quickstart system.
- convex-insights: Query a running Convex app's logs + health in natural language (official MCP): failures, slow/expensive functions, deploy causality — scoped, evidence-backed, with a dashboard deep link.
- convex-launch-readiness: Run every Convex audit (authz, reviewer, advisor, insights) into one scored, deduped readiness report with an ordered fix plan — Lighthouse for your backend.
- convex-migrate: Migrate schema + backfill data on a deployed Convex app using @convex-dev/migrations.
- convex-migrate-rehearse: Rehearse a live-app schema change + backfill on a snapshot-seeded preview deployment, verify, then promote the proven change to prod with the snapshot as rollback.
- convex-monitor: Watch for the next dev/prod error or request in a Convex app and react to it.
- convex-optimize: Audit and optimize an existing Convex app: security, scale, upgrades, observability.
- convex-quickstart: Get a barebones Convex + web template running from a one-sentence idea.
- convex-reviewer: Convex code reviewer — security, auth, validators, performance, and pattern checks for code in a convex/ directory. Use to review or audit Convex functions before shipping.
- convex-seed: Seed or import data into the Convex database.
- convex-self-heal: Production error → triaged, root-caused, repaired, and certified (tsc + rehearsal + reproduce-then-gone) fix PR for a human to merge — then confirm the error stops recurring. Never auto-merges.
- convex-sentinel: Set up Sentinel production error capture in your own Convex deployment.
- convex-ship: Publish the current Convex app to a live *.convex.app URL (deploy backend + upload web build).
- convex-suggest: Suggest the matching Convex component when the user hand-rolls a pattern it already solves (crons, sharded-counter, rate-limiter, storage, search, presence, workflow, RAG, prosemirror-sync). Passive — suggest after the task, never interrupt. Never install without consent.
- convex-test: Generate convex-test tests for the app's Convex functions.
- convex-verify: Prove a Convex feature works — seed, drive as multiple mocked users via convex-test, assert behavior including the negative authz cases (wrong user refused, data-scope enforced).
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

/**
 * Tool-calling + analysis eval for a small local model (e.g. LFM2.5-2.6B),
 * the candidate engine for signed-out / free mode.
 *
 * Every other script in `evals/` talks to the hosted Portkey gateway with a
 * bare system+user body and never passes `tools`. None of them can answer the
 * only question that matters for a 2.6B on-device model: *can it drive the
 * `quote_passage` tool?* That tool is what pins an editor's note to a real
 * passage; a model that cannot call it produces unanchored notes, which is a
 * different (worse) product, not a slightly weaker one.
 *
 * So this script runs the REAL production path rather than an approximation:
 * the prompts from `convex/agentPrompts`, the tool from `convex/agentTools`,
 * `generateText` with `stopWhen: stepCountIs(3)` exactly as
 * `src/utils/ai-client.ts` does. What it changes is only the endpoint.
 *
 * Two runs per case, so tool competence and analysis competence are separable:
 *   - `tools`   — the real path, with `quote_passage` offered.
 *   - `notools` — same prompts, no tool. The control. If analysis is fine here
 *                 and collapses in `tools`, the tool is the problem, not the
 *                 model's reading of the draft.
 *
 * Output is written to two places:
 *   - `evals/local-model-scores.json` — per-case tool metrics + the aggregate.
 *   - `evals/local-model-runs.json`   — `{case_id, output}[]`, the exact shape
 *     `evals/judge.ts` reads. Copy it over `evals/runs.json` and run
 *     `bun run eval:judge` to score analysis quality against the same
 *     faithfulness/helpfulness rubrics used for the hosted models, so the
 *     small model is compared on the incumbent's terms.
 *
 * Serving the model — anything OpenAI-compatible works. llama.cpp needs
 * `--jinja` or it will not emit tool calls at all:
 *   llama-server -hf LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF --jinja -c 8192
 *
 * Usage:
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080/v1 bun run eval:local
 *
 * Env:
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_BASE_URL  default http://localhost:8080/v1
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_ID        default LFM2.5-2.6B
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_API_KEY   default "local" (llama.cpp ignores it)
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_TIMEOUT   ms, default 180000 — CPU decode is slow, be patient
 *
 * Read-only w.r.t. the repo otherwise: only writes the two files above.
 */

import { dirname, resolve } from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

import { createOpenAI } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { generateText, stepCountIs, type ToolSet } from "ai";

import {
  buildSystemPrompt,

  type AgentPersona,
  type AgentRequest,
} from "../convex/agentPrompts";
import { buildQuoteTools } from "../convex/agentTools";
import { PERSONAS } from "../src/utils/personas";
import {
  hasReasoningTags,
  stripReasoningTags,
} from "../src/utils/reasoning-tags";

const HERE = dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
const DATASET_PATH = resolve(HERE, "dataset.jsonl");
const SCORES_PATH = resolve(HERE, "local-model-scores.json");
const RUNS_PATH = resolve(HERE, "local-model-runs.json");

## Verdict

The code is in good shape — clean `tsc`, clean lint, full production build passes. **Not release-ready yet**, but only for process reasons, not code quality.

### Gates checked

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `tsc --noEmit` (clean, no incremental cache) | pass |
| `bun run build` (types + lint + client + ssr) | pass (2 pre-existing warnings in `routes/downloads`) |
| New tests, run individually | 14 pass |
| Full `bun test` | 853 pass, 6 fail — see below |
| `fmt.check` | 3 of the changed files fail |
| `bumpy status` | **no pending bump file** |

## Before you cut the release

1. **No bump file.** `.bumpy/still-warm-press.md` is the empty post-0.11.0 placeholder. You need `bun run release:add` describing this work, or `release:version` has nothing to consume. Version is still 0.11.0.

2. **Prettier on the new files.** `src/utils/generation-stream.ts`, `ai-client-reasoning.test.ts`, `generation-stream.test.ts` fail `fmt.check`. The repo is already dirty repo-wide (117 files), so this isn't a hard gate — but these are yours.

3. **`rubric-panel.tsx` is 862/841 lines of diff for 39/18 lines of real change** — the rest is a whole-file prettier reformat. It'll bury the actual change (`(partial) => …` → `(snapshot) => snapshot.text`) in review and in the changelog. Worth deciding if that's intended before it lands in a release commit.

4. **Test failures** — all pre-existing or environmental, none caused by this work, but one is now staler:
   - 4 new `ai-client-reasoning.test.ts` failures + 1 `ai-client.test.ts` failure appear **only in the full suite** — the known `mock.module` cross-file interference. Pass individually.
   - `personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts` **fails at HEAD too** (I verified by stashing). It's a source-string matcher, and your change makes one more of its assertions stale: it asserts `store.streamingReplies[feedback.noteId],` which is now `…[feedback.noteId]\n.text,`. Since it's already red and this change touches exactly what it asserts, now is the moment to fix or delete it.

## Review notes on the change itself

The core is sound. The reasoning-policy inversion — regenerate only when nothing visible survives, rather than on sight of a `<think>` tag — is applied consistently across `ai-client.ts`, `runLlm`, and `runPlainLlm`, and it halves cost on models whose template always opens a think block. `personaNoteStreams` faithfully mirrors the proven `interviewStreams` pattern (internal write, auth-checked list/clear, same indexes plus `personaId`).

Four things worth knowing:

- **Per-delta `runMutation` in `streamNote`** is one DB write per token chunk, now ×5 personas concurrently. It matches the shipped interview pattern, but that one is single-stream; a convened room is ~1000+ mutations. The dedup only catches byte-identical snapshots. A ~100ms per-persona time throttle would cut this hard with no visible difference. Not a blocker, but the cost is real.
- **`publish(…, "error")` is never called** — there's no try/catch around the stream loop, so a mid-stream failure leaves the row at `"running"`. Harmless in practice (the client's `finally` clears both the store and the rows), but it's dead code that reads like a handled case.
- **Multi-step + tools**: with `stopWhen: stepCountIs(3)`, the accumulator sums text-deltas across *all* steps while `await streamed.text` returns only the last step's. If a model emits prose before calling `quote_passage`, the streamed card shows more than the filed note. The comment in `streamNote` says a step boundary doesn't change what the reader sees — that's not strictly true. Rare and low severity.
- **`runPersona` gained a `streamId` arg that no client passes** (both callers omit it). Fine if it's groundwork for a follow-up; otherwise it's plumbing to nowhere.
- **Orphaned rows**: closing the tab mid-generation skips `clear`, and there's no cron sweep (none for `interviewStreams` either). Consistent with what's there, but it's 5 rows per abandoned convene now.

Want me to do the prettier pass, fix the rotted wiring test, and draft the bump file?

# Changelog







## 0.11.0
<sub>2026-08-05</sub>

-  *(minor)*
  Twyne grows a way out of the browser, a canonical home for published work, and
  an honest account of what its editors are doing — none of it at the cost of the
  draft leaving the machine it was written on.

  **The room, from your own tools.** A `twyne` CLI and a `twyne-mcp` server talk
  to a single token-scoped endpoint, so folios, feedback, and citations are
  reachable from a terminal or from another agent. Personal access tokens are
  created in Settings and stored only as a SHA-256 digest — the token itself is
  shown once and never again. Every operation resolves that digest and then runs
  bound to the verified owner, so a token cannot reach anyone else's work. Writes
  carry the revision they read: a folio that moved in the meantime comes back as
  a conflict rather than quietly overwriting the newer draft.

  **Published pieces get an address.** Publishing files a Standard.site
  publication and document in the writer's own ATProto repository, and Twyne now
  serves the matching reading pages, so a published piece has a canonical,
  verifiable home instead of only a record in a PDS. The share panel remembers
  the record key locally, which is what makes re-publishing and unpublishing work

# @varlock/bumpy 🐸 A modern package versioning, release, and changelog generation tool. Built for monorepos, but works great in simple projects too. ## How It Works Bumpy uses **bump files** (you may know them as "changesets" if coming from [that tool 🦋](https://github.com/changesets/changesets)) - small markdown files that declare an _intent to release packages_ with a bump level (patch/minor/major), and a description that ends up in changelogs. Developers create these files as part of their PRs, and these files are then used to consolidate changes, generate changelogs, and trigger publishing. - Devs/agents create bump files as part of their PRs (using `bumpy add` or manually) - A git hook (pre-commit or pre-push) can enforce bump files exist for changed packages - In CI, a workflow checks PRs for bump files, leaves a comment on the PR detailing changed packages - As PRs merge to the base branch, a "release PR" is kept up to date - Shows what packages will be released and their changelogs (incl. those bumped via dep relationships) - When release PR is merged, publishing is triggered - Pending bump files are deleted and packages are published with updated versions and changelogs, github tags+releases created All of this is automated via two simple GitHub Actions workflows (see [actions guide](https://github.com/dmno-dev/bumpy/blob/main/docs/github-actions.md)). Or can be triggered locally. ### Example bump file `.bumpy/add-user-language.md`: ```markdown --- '@myorg/core': minor '@myorg/utils': patch --- Added user lang prefs to core config. Fixed locale fallback logic in utils. ``` ## Features - **All package managers** - npm, pnpm, yarn, and bun workspaces. With full `workspace:` and `catalog:` support - **Smart dependency propagation** - configurable rules for how version bumps cascade through your dependency graph (see [version propagation docs](https://github.com/dmno-dev/bumpy/blob/main/docs/version-propagation.md)) - **OIDC + staged publishing** - supports OIDC, provenance, [npm staged publishing](https://docs.npmjs.com/staged-publishing) - **Custom release targets** - Per-package custom publish commands let you target anything - VSCode extensions, Docker images, JSR, private registries, etc. - **Flexible package management** - include/exclude any package individually via per-package config, glob patterns, or `privatePackages` setting - **Non-interactive CLI** - `bumpy add` works fully non-interactively for CI/CD and AI-assisted development - **Aggregated GitHub releases** - optionally create a single consolidated release instead of one per package - **Prerelease channels** - branch-based `@next` / `@beta` release lines where prerelease versions are derived at publish time, never committed to git (see [prerelease channels docs](https://github.com/dmno-dev/bumpy/blob/main/docs/prereleases.md)) - **Auto-generate from commits** - `bumpy generate` creates bump files from branch commits - works with any commit style, with enhanced detection for conventional commits - **Pluggable changelog formatters** - built-in `"default"` and `"github"` formatters, or write your own - **Zero runtime dependencies** - dependencies are minimal and bundled at release time - **No additional action/app needed** - no external github action or app to audit and trust ## Getting Started ```bash # Install bun add -d @varlock/bumpy # or npm/pnpm/yarn # Initialize (creates .bumpy/ directory and config, migrates from changesets if applicable) bunx bumpy init # Interactive guidance setting up CI bunx bumpy ci setup # Create a bump file bunx bumpy add # Preview the release plan bunx bumpy status ```

The room writes where you can see it, and models that think first stop costing
twice.

**Hosted notes arrive as they are written.** Convening the room without your own
API key used to mean five blank cards and a wait, because the server generated
each note in full before returning it. The hosted path now streams: each editor
publishes their note as it is composed, keyed by persona, so five cards fill in
at once and the wait is spent reading rather than watching a spinner. The panel
cannot tell whether a note came from your key or from ours — both paths deliver
the same snapshots into the same cards.

**Thinking is shown, not hidden or punished.** A model that reasons before
answering now says so — the card reads "thinking…" and offers the scratch work
folded away, instead of sitting empty for as long as the model works. And a
reply that opened a `<think>` block is no longer thrown away and asked for
again: the thinking was already stripped from what you read, so the second call
bought nothing. Twyne only regenerates when nothing visible survived at all,
which halves the cost and the wait on exactly the models that can least afford
either.

**A harness for small local models.** `bun run eval:local` runs the real
production path — the same prompts, the same `quote_passage` tool — against any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with and without tools, so a candidate on-device
model can be judged on whether it can actually anchor a note to a passage.

Both housekeeping items are done — details at the end. First, the three questions.

## 1. What "per-delta" actually means

`streamNote` (`convex/agents.ts:308-355`) reads the provider stream and writes to the database **inside the loop, awaited**:

```ts
for await (const part of streamed.fullStream) {
  case "text-delta":
    await publish(accumulator.push({type:"text-delta", text: part.text}), "running");
```

and `publish` ends in `await target.ctx.runMutation(internal.personaNoteStreams.write, …)`. That mutation (`convex/personaNoteStreams.ts:52-77`) does an indexed lookup plus a `patch` — a full database transaction, committed, before the loop reads the next chunk from the model.

So every token chunk costs one round trip to the DB. Three consequences:

- **Volume.** `maxTokens` is 380, and `conveneRoom` runs the personas under `Promise.all` (`convex/agents.ts:1314`, `1357`), so a single convene is up to ~1,900 mutations from one action. The dedup guard only skips writes where text *and* reasoning are byte-identical — that catches step boundaries and tool-call parts, not real tokens.
- **Backpressure.** Because the write is awaited, the provider stream isn't drained while the transaction commits. Tokens aren't lost (they buffer), but the note finishes measurably later than an unthrottled read would.
- **Nobody sees the difference.** The rows reach the browser over the websocket subscription and paint on a frame. Anything past ~60 writes/sec is invisible.

The browser path already solved this — `runOnce` in `src/utils/ai-client.ts` runs the same `fullStream` loop but pushes through `createFrameCoalescer`, which delivers at most one snapshot per animation frame. The server path skipped that step. It's why I flagged it: the accumulator stays per-delta (it must, to parse `<think>` across chunk boundaries), but `publish` should be time-gated — write if >100ms since the last one for this persona, always write the final. Roughly:

```ts
let lastWrite = 0;
// …in publish, before the runMutation:
if (status === "running" && Date.now() - lastWrite < 100) return;
lastWrite = Date.now();
```

That takes ~1,900 writes down to ~50 with no visible change. To be clear about precedent: the shipped interview path does the same per-delta thing (`convex/agents.ts:909`), so this isn't a regression — it's an existing pattern now running at 5× concurrency.

## 2. What `streamId` is for

Not errors. It's a **correlation key**, and it exists because a Convex action has no way to push to the browser.

An action returns exactly once, at the end. The only live server→client channel is a query subscription over the database. So "show me the note as it's written" has to be: action writes rows → client subscribes to a query over those rows. For the client to subscribe *before* the run has produced anything, it has to know the key in advance — so the browser mints it (`personas-panel.tsx:744`), subscribes to `personaNoteStreams.list({streamId})`, and only then calls the action with the same id.

It does three jobs:

- **Rendezvous.** Ties the rows the action writes to the query the client is already watching.
- **Scoping.** Row identity is `userId + streamId + personaId`, so two convenes in two tabs don't bleed into each other, and `clear({streamId})` deletes exactly this run's rows and no one else's.
- **Feature flag.** It's `v.optional`. No `streamId` → the old one-shot `generateText` path, no writes at all. That's what keeps the `@twyne/tools` CLI and MCP callers from paying for streaming they can't watch.

The `status: "error"` field is a separate thing and is the dead part I mentioned — nothing ever writes it, because there's no try/catch around the stream loop. On failure the row just stops updating at `"running"` and the client's `finally` cleans up.

## 3. Yes, there's a real reasoning stream — in exactly one panel

**It renders in the Room of Editors** (`personas-panel.tsx:2233-2263`): the status label flips between `thinking…` and `writing…` off `snapshot.activePart`, and when `snapshot.reasoning` is non-empty a `<details>` appears with the scratch work under a `thinking`/`thought` summary — collapsed by default.

Two different provider behaviours feed it, reconciled in the accumulator (`src/utils/generation-stream.ts:42-58`): providers with a native reasoning channel emit `reasoning-delta` parts, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints inline `<think>…</think>` in the text, which `extractTaggedReasoning` pulls back out. Both land in `snapshot.reasoning`, deduped if a provider somehow does both. This is why the loops read `fullStream` instead of `textStream` — `textStream` drops the first kind and leaks the second.

**It does not render anywhere else.** These all take `snapshot.text` and drop the reasoning on the floor:

- `comments-panel.tsx:400` — editor reply
- `rubric-panel.tsx:573` — proof-desk review
- `personas-panel.tsx:1049` — the synthesis card
- reply threads keep the whole snapshot in `streamingReplies` but render only `.text`

So the plumbing is universal and the UI is one panel. Given that the rubric review and the synthesis are the *longest* waits in the app, that asymmetry looks more like "hasn't gotten there yet" than a decision — worth confirming which it is before release.

content.text:
## No — it's the model's output, not the author's

The chunks are **tokens coming back from the LLM** while an editor persona composes their note. Nothing in this path is triggered by the human typing.

Two completely separate flows:

**The author's draft** — untouched by this change. Typing goes to IndexedDB locally, and the push to Convex is debounced at `PUSH_DEBOUNCE_MS = 4_000` (`src/utils/convex-sync.ts:142`) via a `markDirty()` timer that coalesces — `if (pushTimer) return; // already scheduled`. So a minute of continuous typing is on the order of 15 writes, not one per keystroke. There's even a second throttle on top for activity pings, at 2 minutes.

**A persona's note being generated** — the new path. You click "convene the room", the action calls the model, and the model streams its answer back a chunk at a time. Each of *those* chunks triggers a write, so the browser can watch the note appear instead of staring at a blank card for 20 seconds.

So the sequence is:

```
model emits "The opening " → write row → websocket → card repaints
model emits "overclaims"   → write row → websocket → card repaints
model emits ", and the "   → write row → websocket → card repaints
```

The ~1,900 figure is: up to 380 output tokens per note × 5 personas running concurrently under `Promise.all`. It's bounded by `maxTokens`, it only happens while a generation is in flight, and it costs nothing when nobody convenes the room. That's why I called it a scaling note rather than a blocker — it's not an idle-time or typing-time cost, it's a burst during a generation.

The reason it's still worth the 5-line throttle: those writes buy nothing past ~60/second, because the browser can only paint once per frame either way. The BYOK path already recognises this — same loop, but snapshots go through `createFrameCoalescer` before touching the store. The server path just never got the equivalent.

content.text:
Fixed, and the audit turned up worse than what I fixed.

## What I changed

Added `createPublishGate` to `src/utils/generation-stream.ts` — the clock-based sibling of `createFrameCoalescer` that's already there for the browser. It folds the existing dedup together with a cadence limit and returns a simple "is this write worth the trip." Terminal snapshots always pass, so nothing accumulated between the last write and the finish is lost.

Wired into both streaming paths in `convex/agents.ts` at `STREAM_PUBLISH_INTERVAL_MS = 100`:

- `streamNote` (the new persona path) — replaced the inline dedup, dropping `~1,900` writes per convene to `~400`.
- **the interview turn loop** (`agents.ts:909`) — this was already shipped and had *no* dedup at all, writing on every text-delta, reasoning-delta, and reasoning-end. Same gate, same one-line guard.

7 new tests drive an injected clock rather than sleeping. Verified: `tsc` clean, `bun run build` clean, 56 tests pass across the four affected files.

## Other write/transaction problems — yes, and one is serious

**1. `sync.pushAll` re-reads the whole table inside a loop** — `convex/sync.ts:792-800`:

```ts
for (const r of args.personaReplies) {
  const existing = await ctx.db.query("personaReplies")
    .withIndex("by_userId", q => q.eq("userId", userId)).collect();   // ← inside the loop
  const dup = existing.find(row => row.replyId === r.replyId);
```

N replies pushed × N replies collected = **N² document reads in one transaction**. At 200 replies that's 40,000 reads per sync. Convex enforces a `documentsRead` transaction limit, so this doesn't degrade — it starts throwing, and it takes the entire sync down with it, including the draft HTML. It's in the path that fires every 4 seconds while someone types. The fix is to hoist the `collect` out of the loop into a `Set` of `replyId`s, two lines. Every sibling loop in that function already uses a proper indexed `.first()`; this one is the odd one out.

**2. `pushAll` writes everything, unconditionally.** `PUSH_DEBOUNCE_MS = 4_000`, and `buildLocalSnapshot` assembles the *entire* local state — every brief, every folio's full draft HTML, every note, every reply, every rubric result, the whole bibliography. `pushAll` then patches each row whether or not it changed. Typing one character in folio A rewrites the HTML of folios B, C and D and re-patches every note you've ever received. `state.lastSnapshot` is assigned on every push (`convex-sync.ts:405`) and **never read** — the hook for diffing is sitting there unused.

**3. Three tables hold one giant document each.** `folios: v.array(v.any())`, `customPersonas: v.array(v.any())`, `bibliographies.entries: v.array(v.any())`. Your own Convex guidelines call this out by name at `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md:188` — unbounded arrays inside a document hit the 1MB limit, and every update rewrites the whole document. Bibliography is the one that grows without a ceiling.

**4. No cleanup for either stream table.** `interviewStreams` and now `personaNoteStreams` orphan their rows if a tab closes mid-generation. No cron exists. Low urgency, but it only ever grows.

None of 1–4 is caused by this release's work — all are pre-existing. But **#1 is a latent outage in the sync path**, and it's a two-line fix. Want me to take it, and the `lastSnapshot` diffing in #2, before you cut 0.12.0?

# Data & sync architecture How a sentence typed in the editor reaches the database, what else writes to that database, and where the arrangement is stranger than it looks. Written against the working tree as of the 0.12.0 release preparation. Findings are listed at the end with their status. --- ## C4 L1 — System context ```mermaid flowchart TD writer["Writer
person"] reader["Reader
person, unauthenticated"] twyne["Twyne
Local-first writing desk with
a room of editorial personas"] llm["LLM providers
writer's own key, or hosted"] pds["ATProto PDS
Standard.site records"] creem["Creem
subscriptions"] obs["Arize / PostHog
traces, product events"] tools["twyne CLI + MCP server
token-scoped"] writer -->|"drafts, convenes the room"| twyne reader -->|"reads /handle/slug"| twyne tools -->|"HTTP, personal access token"| twyne twyne -->|"generation, streamed"| llm twyne -->|"publishes records"| pds twyne -->|"webhooks in, checkout out"| creem twyne -->|"spans and events"| obs ``` ## C4 L2 — Containers ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph browser["Browser"] spa["Qwik SPA
editor, panels, routes"] idb[("IndexedDB
session source of truth")] lix[("Lix store
versioned draft blocks")] ls[("localStorage
settings, BYOK keys")] end subgraph convex["Convex deployment"] q["Queries
reactive reads"] m["Mutations
transactional writes"] a["Actions
LLM calls, side effects"] http["HTTP router
/api/integrations/v1, webhooks"] cron["Crons
stream sweep"] db[("Document DB
31 tables")] end spa <--> idb spa <--> lix spa <--> ls spa -->|"pushAll, debounced 4s"| m spa -->|"per-entity mutations"| m spa -->|"pullAll on sign-in"| q spa -->|"onUpdate subscriptions"| q spa -->|"conveneRoom, runPersona"| a a -->|"runMutation"| m m --> db q --> db cron --> m http --> m http --> q ``` The important asymmetry: **IndexedDB is the source of truth for the current session; Convex is the source of truth across sessions.** Nothing in the editor blocks on the network, and a signed-out writer never touches Convex at all. ## C4 L3 — Inside the sync component ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph sync["src/utils/convex-sync.ts"] dirty["markDirty()
coalescing 4s timer"] build["buildLocalSnapshot()
reads all of IndexedDB + Lix"] payload["buildPushPayload()
maps to the wire shape"] diff["diffPushPayload()
vs. last acknowledged push"] push["pushLocalSnapshot()"] last[("state.lastPushed
set only on success")] hydrate["handleUserChanged()
pullAll then newer-wins merge"] end edits["editor / panels"] -->|"any local change"| dirty dirty -->|"at most every 4s"| push push --> build --> payload --> diff diff -->|"nothing moved"| noop["no network call"] diff -->|"changed sections only"| pushAll["sync.pushAll"] pushAll -->|"resolved"| last last -.->|"compared against"| diff signin["sign-in / account swap"] --> hydrate hydrate --> pushAll ``` `lastPushed` is the whole trick. It holds the payload the server has **acknowledged**, not the one last built — so a push that threw leaves it untouched and the next push carries the entire gap. It starts null on sign-in, which is what makes the account-seeding path send everything. --- ## Where each kind of data actually lives | Data | Local home | Convex table | Written by | Cadence | |---|---|---|---|---| | Draft HTML | IndexedDB + Lix | `folioContent` | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s, only if changed | | Folio list | IndexedDB | `folios` (one row, array) | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | | Dossier / brief | IndexedDB + Lix file | `briefs` | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | | Persona notes | IndexedDB | `personaNotes` | snapshot push **and** `putPersonaNote` | on file + every 4s | | Replies | IndexedDB | `personaReplies` | snapshot push **and** `addPersonaReply` | on send + every 4s | | Rubric results | IndexedDB | `rubricResults` | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | | Bibliography | Lix file | `bibliographies` (one row, array) | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | | Custom personas | IndexedDB | `customPersonas` (one row, array) | snapshot push **and** `putCustomPersonas` | on edit + every 4s | | Room settings | IndexedDB | `roomSettings` | `putRoomSettings` only | on change | | Theme | IndexedDB | `appearance` | `putAppearance` only | on change | | AI / writer settings | localStorage + IDB | — | never synced | — | | Notes being generated | — | `personaNoteStreams` | server action | ≤ 10/s per persona | | Interview turn | — | `dossierInterviewStreams` | server action | ≤ 10/s | | Presence | — | `presence` | heartbeat | every 3s while collaborating | | Writing streak | — | `writingActivity` | `recordActivity` | throttled to 2 min | | Published pieces | — | `published` + PDS | publish flow | on publish | | Lix snapshot blob | IndexedDB | `lixBlobs` | **nothing** (see finding 9) | never | ## Sequence — signing in ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant B as Browser participant IDB as IndexedDB participant C as Convex B->>IDB: buildLocalSnapshot() Note over B: lastPushed stays null —
nothing has reached the server yet B->>C: sync.pullAll C-->>B: remote snapshot alt server is empty B->>C: sync.pushAll (everything) Note over B,C: seeds the account else server has data B->>IDB: merge, newer-wins per slice by updatedAt B->>C: sync.pushAll (everything, first push) end Note over B: lastPushed set on the ack ``` There is no CRDT and no operational transform. The merge is per-slice newer-wins, and it runs **only at sign-in** — not continuously. ## Sequence — steady-state typing ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant E as Editor participant S as convex-sync participant C as Convex E->>S: markDirty() on every keystroke Note over S: first call arms a 4s timer;
later calls are swallowed S->>S: buildLocalSnapshot + buildPushPayload S->>S: diff against lastPushed alt only folio f2's draft moved S->>C: pushAll{folioContent:[f2]} C-->>S: ok Note over S: lastPushed := payload else nothing moved Note over S: no network call at all end ``` ## Sequence — a convened room, streaming ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Personas panel participant C as Convex participant A as conveneRoom action participant M as LLM P->>P: streamId = crypto.randomUUID() P->>C: onUpdate(personaNoteStreams.list, {streamId}) P->>A: conveneRoom({streamId, ...}) par five editors at once A->>M: streamText (persona 1..5) loop tokens M-->>A: text-delta / reasoning-delta Note over A: accumulate every delta;
write at most 10x/sec A->>C: personaNoteStreams.write C-->>P: subscription push → card repaints end end A-->>P: filed notes P->>C: personaNoteStreams.clear({streamId}) Note over C: rows the browser never cleared
are swept hourly by age ``` The action cannot push to the browser — it returns once, at the end. Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Twyne · Architecture reference

Data & sync: where the words actually go

How a sentence typed in the editor reaches the database, what else writes to that database, and where the arrangement is stranger than it looks.

Working tree at 0.12.0 prep 31 tables 13 findings · 4 fixed · 9 open

System context

Twyne is local-first. A signed-out writer never touches Convex; a signed-in one treats it as the store that survives the session, not the one the editor waits on.

Containers

The load-bearing asymmetry. IndexedDB is the source of truth for the current session; Convex is the source of truth across sessions. Everything odd below follows from that split being maintained by convention rather than by a protocol.

Inside the sync component

lastPushed is the whole trick. It holds the payload the server has acknowledged, not the one last built — so a push that threw leaves it untouched and the next push carries the entire gap. It starts null on sign-in, which is what makes the account-seeding path send everything.

Where each kind of data lives

Storage map
DataLocal homeConvex tableWritten byCadence
Draft HTMLIndexedDB + LixfolioContentsnapshot push≤ 4s, if changed
Folio listIndexedDBfolios — one row, arraysnapshot push≤ 4s
Dossier / briefIndexedDB + Lixbriefssnapshot push≤ 4s
Persona notesIndexedDBpersonaNotessnapshot push and putPersonaNoteon file + 4s
RepliesIndexedDBpersonaRepliessnapshot push and addPersonaReplyon send + 4s
Rubric resultsIndexedDBrubricResultssnapshot push≤ 4s
BibliographyLix filebibliographies — one row, arraysnapshot push≤ 4s
Custom personasIndexedDBcustomPersonas — one row, arraysnapshot push and putCustomPersonason edit + 4s
Room settingsIndexedDBroomSettingsputRoomSettings onlyon change
ThemeIndexedDBappearanceputAppearance onlyon change
AI / writer settingslocalStorage + IDB—never synced—
Notes being generated—personaNoteStreamsserver action≤ 10/s per persona
Interview turn—dossierInterviewStreamsserver action≤ 10/s
Presence—presenceheartbeatevery 3s
Writing streak—writingActivityrecordActivitythrottled to 2 min
Published pieces—published + PDSpublish flowon publish
Lix snapshot blobIndexedDBlixBlobsnothing — see finding 9never

Signing in

There is no CRDT and no operational transform. The merge is per-slice newer-wins, and it runs only at sign-in — not continuously.

Steady-state typing

A convened room, streaming

The action cannot push to the browser — it returns once, at the end. The database is the only live channel, which is the entire reason streamId exists: the client mints it, subscribes, then calls the action.

Write-cadence budget

Everything that writes on a timer
WriterTriggerPeak rate
pushAlltyping≤ 15/min, changed rows only
personaNoteStreamsconvened room≤ 10/s × 5 personas
dossierInterviewStreamsinterview turn≤ 10/s
presencecollaborating20/min per participant
writingActivitytyping0.5/min
rateBucketsany rate-limited call1 per call
stream sweepcron≤ 400 deletes/hour

The 1.5s and 4s intervals in collaboration.ts and share-dialog.tsx are local polls — Lix state and a dialog refresh — not network writes.

Findings

  1. 01

    Streaming wrote once per token Fixed

    Both streamNote and the interview turn loop awaited a Convex mutation inside for await (const part of fullStream). A convened room was up to ~1,900 transactions, and the awaited write applied backpressure to reading the provider stream. Now gated by createPublishGate at 100ms — the clock-based sibling of the browser's createFrameCoalescer — which cuts it ~5× with no visible difference, since the reader repaints on a frame either way. Terminal snapshots always pass the gate.

  2. 02

    Quadratic reads in the sync mutation Fixed

    pushAll re-collected the entire replies table inside its own per-reply loop. N replies pushed × N collected, in one transaction, in the path that fires every 4 seconds. Past a few hundred replies this stops being slow and starts exceeding the transaction read limit — taking the draft sync down with it. Now one collect and a Set, hoisted out of the loop.

  3. 03

    Every push wrote everything Fixed

    Four seconds of typing rewrote every folio's HTML, every note, every reply and every rubric result, whether or not any of it had moved. state.lastSnapshot was assigned on every push and never read. Now lastPushed, diffed per section and set only on acknowledgement — so a failed push is carried by the next one rather than silently skipped.

  4. 04

    Abandoned stream rows accumulated forever Fixed

    A tab closed mid-generation never ran clear. Added by_updatedAt indexes to both stream tables, an hourly cron, and a bounded sweep.

  5. 05

    Four tables hold one giant document each Open

    folios, customPersonas, bibliographies.entries and lixBlobs.blob are single rows containing an entire collection. Every change rewrites the whole document, and Convex caps a document at 1MB. convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md:188 names this exact anti-pattern. The bibliography grows without a ceiling; the Lix blob is an entire SQLite database in a v.bytes() column. This is a schema migration, not a patch — deliberately not attempted mid-release.

  6. 06

    Two write paths reach the same tables Open

    Persona notes, replies and custom personas are written both by the bulk snapshot push and by granular mutations called straight from components. Nothing coordinates them; last writer wins. Not currently corrupting anything, because both write the same content from the same local state — but it is two sources of truth for one row.

  7. 07

    The snapshot sync has no delete channel Open

    pushAll only ever upserts. A row deleted locally through a path that does not call the matching remove* mutation stays on the server, and pullAll hands it back on the next sign-in. Deletions are only durable when they go through the granular mutation.

  8. 08

    Merging happens once, at sign-in Open

    Two devices open at the same time do not reconcile: neither subscribes to its own data, so each pushes over the other and neither sees the change until a reload. The reactive subscriptions that exist are for generation streams and collaboration presence only.

  9. 09

    The Lix blob sync is dead code Open

    syncToConvex and loadFromConvex are exported from convex-sync.ts and referenced by nothing but their own test. The lixBlobs table therefore has no writer in production.

  10. 10

    streamNote can never write its error status Open

    There is no try/catch around the stream loop, so a mid-generation failure leaves the row at "running". Harmless today — the client's finally clears both the store and the rows — but the branch reads like a handled case and is not one.

  11. 11

    Streamed and filed text can disagree under multi-step Open

    With stopWhen: stepCountIs(3), the accumulator sums text-deltas across all steps while await streamed.text returns only the last step's. A model that emits prose before calling quote_passage would show more in the card than lands in the note. Rare; low severity.

  12. 12

    runPersona accepts a streamId no caller passes Open

    Both call sites omit it, so the single-persona hosted path is plumbed for streaming that never happens. Fine as groundwork; dead otherwise.

  13. 13

    personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts is red on main Open

    A source-string matcher that has rotted, and this cycle's changes make one more of its assertions stale. Failing before any of this work began.

content.text:
**https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f7af9af6-a90f-4beb-9578-38eeff246eb3** — six mermaid diagrams (C4 L1/L2/L3 + three sequences), the storage map, the write-cadence budget, and all 13 findings. Same content also lives in the repo at `docs/architecture/data-and-sync.md`. Palette is Twyne's own Editorial/Nightpress tokens from `theme.ts`, so it follows the viewer's theme.

## The fixes you asked for

**Quadratic reads** (`convex/sync.ts`) — the `collect` is hoisted out of the per-reply loop into a `Set`, which also guards against a payload carrying the same reply twice. One read per sync instead of N.

**Diffed pushes** (`src/utils/convex-sync.ts`) — `lastSnapshot` was assigned on every push and never read. It's now `lastPushed`, holding the payload the server **acknowledged**, and the push sends only changed sections. Two details that turned out to matter:

- It's set *after* the mutation resolves. A push that threw leaves it untouched so the next one carries the whole gap — diffing against an unlanded push is how a draft goes missing.
- `handleUserChanged` used to prime it from local state *before* anything was sent. Left as-is, that would have made the diff conclude there was nothing to send on the exact path that seeds a new account. Removed, with a comment saying why.

**Stream cleanup** — `by_updatedAt` on both stream tables, a new `convex/streamSweep.ts` with a bounded 200-row sweep per table, and `convex/crons.ts` running it hourly against anything untouched for an hour.

Plus the earlier throttle now covers the interview path too, which had no dedup at all.

## Verification

`tsc` clean, `bun run build` clean, `convex codegen` picked up both new modules. The sync tests went 7 → 10: two existing ones were asserting the old "every flush writes everything" behavior and now assert on the sign-in push instead, and I added three for the diff — nothing-changed sends nothing, a changed draft sends only that draft, and a failed push is fully resent by the next one. Full suite is 863 pass / 6 fail, the same 6 as before I started.

## Deliberately not done

**Finding 5** — `folios`, `customPersonas`, `bibliographies.entries` and `lixBlobs.blob` each hold an entire collection in one document, against your own guidelines at `guidelines.md:188`. That's a schema migration with a data backfill, and slipping it into a release you're about to cut is how the release goes wrong. It's written up as the top open item.

Two things the audit turned up that I'd flag as more interesting than they sound: `syncToConvex`/`loadFromConvex` are referenced by nothing but their own test, so `lixBlobs` has **no writer in production** — and the snapshot sync has no delete channel, so a local deletion that doesn't go through a `remove*` mutation comes back on the next sign-in.

It holds the payload the server has 101 **acknowledged**, not the one last built — so a push that threw leaves it 102 untouched and the next push carries the entire gap. It starts null on sign-in, 103 which is what makes the account-seeding path send everything. 104 105 --- 106 107 ## Where each kind of data actually lives 108 109 | Data | Local home | Convex table | Written by | Cadence | 110 |---|---|---|---|---| 111 | Draft HTML | IndexedDB + Lix | `folioContent` | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s, only if changed | 112 | Folio list | IndexedDB | `folios` (one row, array) | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | 113 | Dossier / brief | IndexedDB + Lix file | `briefs` | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | 114 | Persona notes | IndexedDB | `personaNotes` | snapshot push **and** `putPersonaNote` | on file + every 4s | 115 | Replies | IndexedDB | `personaReplies` | snapshot push **and** `addPersonaReply` | on send + every 4s | 116 | Rubric results | IndexedDB | `rubricResults` | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | 117 | Bibliography | Lix file | `bibliographies` (one row, array) | snapshot push | ≤ every 4s | 118 | Custom personas | IndexedDB | `customPersonas` (one row, array) | snapshot push **and** `putCustomPersonas` | on edit + every 4s | 119 | Room settings | IndexedDB | `roomSettings` | `putRoomSettings` only | on change | 120 | Theme | IndexedDB | `appearance` | `putAppearance` only | on change | 121 | AI / writer settings | localStorage + IDB | — | never synced | — | 122 | Notes being generated | — | `personaNoteStreams` | server action | ≤ 10/s per persona | 123 | Interview turn | — | `dossierInterviewStreams` | server action | ≤ 10/s | 124 | Presence | — | `presence` | heartbeat | every 3s while collaborating | 125 | Writing streak | — | `writingActivity` | `recordActivity` | throttled to 2 min | 126 | Published pieces | — | `published` + PDS | publish flow | on publish | 127 | Lix snapshot blob | IndexedDB | `lixBlobs` | **nothing** (see finding 9) | never | 128 129 ## Sequence — signing in 130 131 ```mermaid 132 sequenceDiagram 133 participant B as Browser 134 participant IDB as IndexedDB 135 participant C as Convex 136 137 B->>IDB: buildLocalSnapshot() 138 Note over B: lastPushed stays null —
nothing has reached the server yet 139 B->>C: sync.pullAll 140 C-->>B: remote snapshot 141 142 alt server is empty 143 B->>C: sync.pushAll (everything) 144 Note over B,C: seeds the account 145 else server has data 146 B->>IDB: merge, newer-wins per slice by updatedAt 147 B->>C: sync.pushAll (everything, first push) 148 end 149 Note over B: lastPushed set on the ack 150 ``` 151 152 There is no CRDT and no operational transform. The merge is per-slice 153 newer-wins, and it runs **only at sign-in** — not continuously. 154 155 ## Sequence — steady-state typing 156 157 ```mermaid 158 sequenceDiagram 159 participant E as Editor 160 participant S as convex-sync 161 participant C as Convex 162 163 E->>S: markDirty() on every keystroke 164 Note over S: first call arms a 4s timer —

import { defineSchema, defineTable } from "convex/server";
import { v } from "convex/values";

/**
 * One item of a per-user collection.
 *
 * Three collections — folios, custom personas, bibliography entries — used to
 * live as an array inside a single document each. Every edit rewrote the whole
 * document, and the collection could never outgrow Convex's 1MB document cap.
 * These tables replace that arrangement with a row per item.
 *
 * The field and index names are deliberately identical across all three, so a
 * single accessor in `lib/collections.ts` can serve them and they cannot drift
 * apart. `item` stays `v.any()` for the same reason the arrays did: adding a
 * field to a folio should not need a migration.
 */
const collectionEntry = {
  userId: v.string(),
  /** The item's own id, as the client models it. Unique per user per table. */
  itemId: v.string(),
  item: v.any(),
  /** Position in the collection, so the array round-trips in its own order. */
  order: v.number(),
  updatedAt: v.number(),
};

  folioEntries: defineTable(collectionEntry)

toolUseResult.originalFile:
---
twyne: minor
---

The room writes where you can see it, and models that think first stop costing
twice.

**Hosted notes arrive as they are written.** Convening the room without your own
API key used to mean five blank cards and a wait, because the server generated
each note in full before returning it. The hosted path now streams: each editor
publishes their note as it is composed, keyed by persona, so five cards fill in
at once and the wait is spent reading rather than watching a spinner. The panel
cannot tell whether a note came from your key or from ours — both paths deliver
the same snapshots into the same cards.

**Thinking is shown, not hidden or punished.** A model that reasons before
answering now says so — the card reads "thinking…" and offers the scratch work
folded away, instead of sitting empty for as long as the model works. And a
reply that opened a `<think>` block is no longer thrown away and asked for
again: the thinking was already stripped from what you read, so the second call
bought nothing. Twyne only regenerates when nothing visible survived at all,
which halves the cost and the wait on exactly the models that can least afford
either.

**A harness for small local models.** `bun run eval:local` runs the real
production path — the same prompts, the same `quote_passage` tool — against any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with and without tools, so a candidate on-device
model can be judged on whether it can actually anchor a note to a passage.

Both done. ## The mermaid failures A `;` inside `Note over` text terminates the statement in mermaid's sequence grammar, so everything after it — including the `
` — became an unparseable fragment. Only those two notes had semicolons, which is exactly why only those two diagrams failed. Rather than eyeball it, I installed mermaid 11 in a scratch dir and ran every block through the real parser. All six now parse, in both the artifact and the repo markdown. That checker is still in the scratchpad if you want it in CI — it's ~20 lines and would have caught this before publish. Artifact republished at the same URL: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f7af9af6-a90f-4beb-9578-38eeff246eb3** ## The migration The key decision: **the wire contract doesn't change.** `pushAll`/`pullAll`/`putFolios` still take and return whole arrays, because that's what the browser holds. Only the storage underneath became row-per-item. That means zero client protocol changes and nothing to coordinate between frontend and backend deploys. Three new tables — `folioEntries`, `personaEntries`, `bibliographyEntries` — declared from one shared field set in the schema so they can't drift, all behind `convex/lib/collections.ts`. Every call site now goes through `readCollection`/`writeCollection`: `sync.ts` (get/put + both bulk paths), `integrations.ts` (the CLI/MCP API had its own copies of this logic in five places), and `writingActivity.ts`. How the transition is safe: - **Reads fall back** to the legacy document for anyone not yet migrated, so nothing breaks the moment this deploys. - **Writes migrate the user** and drop the legacy row — so there's never a second, staler copy for a reader to find. - **A backfill cron** every 10 minutes converts dormant accounts, bounded to 25 users per collection per pass. `backfillRemaining` tells you when it's safe to retire. - **Migration preserves the collection's `updatedAt`**, so a migrated account doesn't look freshly edited to the sign-in merge and overwrite a device's real work. - **Account deletion** covers the new tables — missing that would have left deleted accounts' work behind. A side benefit: these three collections now have a real delete channel. Their arrays are always sent whole, so an absent item means deleted and its row goes. That's finding 7 half-closed. ## Tests 15 new convex-test cases against a real test database, run with vitest (the convex tests use vitest; `bun test` skips them). They target the ways this specific change loses data silently: order surviving a reorder, an item dropped from the array actually being deleted, only the edited folio's row being rewritten, the legacy document readable before migration and gone after, migration preserving age, **the backfill refusing to overwrite rows a write already migrated**, and omitting a section from a partial push meaning "leave it" rather than "empty it". ## Verification `tsc` clean, `bun run build` clean, `convex codegen` clean. Vitest: 24 pass. `bun test`: 863 pass, the same 6 pre-existing failures. Every file I touched is prettier-clean. Bump file updated; `bumpy status` still reads 0.11.0 → 0.12.0. ## Two things to know **`convex codegen` uploaded to your dev deployment**, so the new tables and functions are live there. Production is untouched until you run a real deploy — and when you do, the backfill cron starts on its own. **I left `lixBlobs` alone.** It has the same one-giant-document problem, but nothing writes it (finding 9) — migrating a table with no writer would be motion without purpose. The real fix there is deleting the dead `syncToConvex`/`loadFromConvex` path, which I'd want your go-ahead on since it removes a table's worth of data. Rollback caveat worth stating plainly: because writes drop the legacy row, rolling back to the previous release would make the server look empty for migrated users. They'd re-seed from IndexedDB on next sign-in — local-first saves you here — but it's not a silent rollback.

# Deploying Twyne

Twyne ships as a Qwik City SSR app. The browser bundle is built by Vite into
`dist/`, the SSR server entry into `server/`, and `server.js` (Node `http`)
serves both and listens on `$PORT`.

## Railway (primary)

The repo is configured for [Railway](https://railway.com) via `railway.json`
(`builder: RAILPACK`) and [`railpack.json`](https://railpack.com) — Railpack is
Railway's successor to Nixpacks:

## Feature flags

Two capabilities ship dark and are switched on through PostHog feature flags
(runtime, per user/environment):

| Flag             | Effect                                                                                                   |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `twyne-pricing`  | Enables the `/pricing` page (Creem) + its nav links. Off ⇒ direct visits redirect home after flags load. |
| `twyne-local-ai` | Surfaces the desktop-only native LiteRT model (Gemma 4 E4B) in the UI.                                   |

Set `PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` and optionally `PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`
(`https://us.i.posthog.com` by default) in the frontend deployment. The legacy
`PUBLIC_FEATURE_PRICING` and `PUBLIC_FEATURE_LOCAL_AI` env vars are fallback
defaults for local/offline builds where PostHog is absent; PostHog should own
production rollout.

PostHog also captures AI Observability events for evals. Browser-side BYOK and
desktop-local model calls emit `$ai_generation` through `posthog-js`; Convex
server-side hosted AI calls emit the same event via the capture API when
`POSTHOG_PROJECT_API_KEY` (and optional `POSTHOG_HOST`) is set in Convex. Create
PostHog evals against `$ai_generation`, then filter/break down by
`twyne_feature`, `$ai_provider`, `$ai_model`, `twyne_persona_id`, and
`twyne_expected_format`.

**Creem** (when pricing is on): set `PUBLIC_CREEM_PRODUCT_PRO` (public product
id) plus the Convex secrets `CREEM_API_KEY`, `CREEM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, and
`CREEM_SUCCESS_URL`. Point a Creem webhook at
`<VITE_CONVEX_SITE_URL>/creem/webhook`. Also set `CREEM_PRO_PRODUCT_IDS` in
Convex (comma-separated) to the product id(s) that grant Pro — this is the
server-side allowlist: checkout rejects any product not in it, and a webhook
event for a non-allowlisted product can never grant Pro.

**Hosted voice** (Pro tier): set `VOICE_OPENAI_API_KEY` in Convex, optionally
`VOICE_OPENAI_MODEL` (defaults to `gpt-4o-mini-tts`) and `VOICE_OPENAI_VOICE`
(defaults to `alloy`). If `VOICE_OPENAI_API_KEY` is unset, hosted voice uses
`OPENAI_API_KEY`. BYOK voice does not use server secrets.

**Local model** (desktop only): the web flag just shows the UI; the model runs
as a native LiteRT-LM server bundled into the Electrobun desktop build. Build
that variant with `TWYNE_DESKTOP_LOCAL_AI=true` and `LOCAL_MODEL_PATH` pointing
at the Gemma 4 E4B LiteRT file. The plain web app never loads the model.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Railway build step: deploy Convex backend (when key is configured), then
# build the Qwik City frontend + SSR server.
#
# Gating: when CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY is unset (frontend-only deploys, preview
# environments, local re-runs) we still build the frontend but skip the
# backend push.

set -euo pipefail

if [ -n "${CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY:-}" ]; then
  echo "==> Deploying Convex backend"
  npx convex deploy --cmd 'bun run build.client && bun run build.server'
else
  echo "==> CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY not set — building frontend only, skipping convex deploy"
  bun run build.client
  bun run build.server
fi

git reset -q docs/architecture && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(ai): stream hosted notes, and store collections a row at a time

Three strands, all in the path between a generation and the database.

**Hosted notes stream.** `conveneRoom` and the interview turn publish
snapshots into `personaNoteStreams` / `dossierInterviewStreams` as they are
written, so the panel fills in rather than jumping. An action cannot push to
the browser, so the client mints a `streamId`, subscribes, and only then calls
the action. Reasoning is surfaced as its own folded-away part instead of being
grounds for discarding the reply: a model that opens a `<think>` block by
template used to cost two calls for every note, and now costs one. Twyne only
regenerates when nothing visible survived.

**Writes are no longer at token rate.** Both stream loops awaited a mutation
per delta — up to ~1,900 transactions for one convened room, with the awaited
write applying backpressure to reading the provider stream. `createPublishGate`
holds them to 10/sec, the clock-based sibling of the browser's frame coalescer.
Abandoned rows are swept hourly by age.

**Sync stops rewriting everything.** `pushAll` re-collected the whole replies
table inside its own per-reply loop — quadratic reads in one transaction, in
the path that fires every 4 seconds, eventually exceeding the transaction read
limit and taking the draft with it. It also wrote every folio, note and reply
on every push regardless of what moved; `lastPushed` now holds what the server
acknowledged and only the difference goes up. It is set after the mutation
resolves, so a push that failed is carried by the next one rather than
diffed away.

**Folios, custom personas and bibliography are rows, not arrays.** Each was one
document holding an entire collection: every edit rewrote the whole thing, and
the collection could not outgrow the 1MB document cap. All three now live a row
per item behind `lib/collections.ts`. The wire contract is unchanged — callers
still hand over and receive whole arrays — so no client protocol moved. Reads
fall back to the legacy document until the backfill reaches a user; writes
migrate that user and drop the legacy row, leaving no staler second copy.
Migration preserves the collection's age so newer-wins keeps its meaning.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
